name: The Alabaster Choir

detectability.signature: Coherent light refracting through kilometer-scale lattice faces; a faint piezoelectric hum at 4 hertz

proximity: Sensor returns fragment into thousands of phantom images off the lattice faces
Piezoelectric fields induce a gentle static charge on passing hulls
contact: Hull contact leaves microscopic seed crystals bonded to the plating
Laser ranging returns arrive as pure, chiming tones
prolonged_exposure: Crystal seeding accelerates on any surface left in sustained contact
Crew report lingering synesthesia, hearing light as sound for days afterward

phenomena: Coherent internal luminescence when struck by starlight
Exotic particles detectable on sensors along growth fronts
hazards: Contamination of hulls and equipment by crystal seeding
Structural compromise from invasive growth in conduits and joints
opportunities: Rare element concentration within the lattice
Unique material synthesis from ethically quarried prisms
known_incidents: The freighter Ledger of Light docked after a close flyby and spent a year shedding alabaster filaments from her coolant lines
Lattice samples grown in orbital labs achieved an optical coherence prized by manufacturers of fine instruments
description: The Alabaster Choir is a spreading reef of translucent crystal some thirty light-seconds across, grown into faceted columns and vaulted galleries that catch starlight and return it in slow colored chords. The lattice is a single contiguous mineral of no catalogued class, humming faintly at four hertz as tidal stresses play across its spans. From a distance it reads as a cathedral abandoned by its builders before consecration.

The formation grows outward at a steady few centimeters per day, adding ribs and spurs in patterns that repeat with near-musical regularity. Surfaces that touch it are seeded: hulls, probes, and tools sprout filaments of the same alabaster within hours. Nothing has ever been observed to break the crystal, only to become more of it.

Spectral dating places the colony's beginnings some three million years past, seeded perhaps by a single shard of interstellar material. The freighter Ledger of Light introduced it to inhabited space accidentally, and decontamination protocols across the sector still bear her name. Materials houses pay dearly for quarried fragments, which is to say for any at all.

Harvest crews work the reef's margin under strict tool quarantine, sawing prisms whose optical purity borders on the unreasonable. Biologists keep testing the lattice for anything resembling intent and keep filing inconclusive results. Sailors passing near at night swear the Choir sings back.
